claims.text: Rapid laser heating combined with in situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray diffraction can determine the melting temperature of high-entropy alloys.
The combined technique can determine the enthalpy and entropy of fusion of high-entropy alloys.
The combined technique can determine the volume change at melting in high-entropy alloys.
The combined technique can determine liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys.
Direct capture of abrupt structural transformations during melting provides the physical basis for the proposed measurements.
Ultrafast laser heating induces a transient state bridging the solid and liquid phases.
Melting produces abrupt diffraction-pattern changes such as disappearance or severe broadening of Bragg peaks.
A laser pulse can raise the alloy temperature past its melting point while synchronized X-ray diffraction records the associated structural evolution.
Correlating sudden diffraction changes with precise temperature measurements yields an accurate melting temperature.
Correlating diffraction changes with temperature measurements and calibrated thermal inputs yields fusion enthalpy and entropy.
Abrupt diffraction-peak shifts permit identification of volume change at melting.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties can be deduced from diffraction-signal characteristics and calibrated thermal inputs.
The proposed method will determine melting temperature with an accuracy of ±5 K.
The proposed method will estimate fusion enthalpy and entropy with errors under ±2% relative to traditional calorimetry.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic-property extraction will be reproducible across typical FCC and BCC high-entropy alloys.
The proposed method is more efficient than traditional differential scanning calorimetry and static X-ray diffraction.
Traditional differential scanning calorimetry and static X-ray diffraction are less capable of capturing rapid transient melting phenomena.
The approach is most applicable to homogeneous high-entropy alloys having relatively simple FCC or BCC structures.
Alloys with complex microstructures or substantial compositional heterogeneity may require adaptation of the method.
Application under extreme pressures may require adaptation beyond the initial experimental design.
